I am 60 this year, and I have farmed these same 6 mu in Quzhou County for 30 years. My wife and I do most of the field work. My son and daughter-in-law work in a factory over in Handan, but they come back for harvest and planting when they can get leave. I finished middle school, so I can read the numbers on the fertilizer bags and I once attended a village training meeting about ten years ago, but honestly I trust my own eyes and what the neighbors do more than anything written on a piece of paper.

It is early October now. I just finished harvesting maize last week and the wheat needs to go into the ground before the cold comes.

For winter wheat, I use an improved variety — not the old local seed, but the kind in the red-and-white bag that I have planted for about five years. I sow about 15 kg of seed per mu, so for 6 mu I buy two 50 kg bags and have a little left over. Before planting, I hire the rotary tiller to work the field once after the maize stubble is chopped. That costs 40 yuan per mu and saves my back.

For fertilizer, I put down one 50 kg bag of compound fertilizer per mu as the base. The bag says 15-15-15, so that is about 7 and a half kilograms each of nitrogen, phosphate, and potash per mu. Then at wheat jointing time in March, I topdress with 20 kg of urea per mu — that is another 9 kg or so of nitrogen. I also broadcast another 5 kg of urea per mu at heading if the crop looks like it needs it. Altogether that is about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu. The county extension fellow once told me 15 kg is enough, but three years ago I tried cutting back and my wheat turned yellow and thin, so now I play it safe. I do not measure the phosphorus and potassium separately — whatever is in the compound bag is what I use, and I buy the same bag every year.

I irrigate wheat three times: once before the winter freeze so the seedlings do not dry out, once at jointing in March, and once at grain filling in May. Pumping water from the well costs me about 35 to 40 yuan per mu each time, so three times is already over 700 yuan just for wheat water, but that is what everyone in the village does and I cannot skip it. I spray pesticide three times: herbicide in early spring, then insecticide or fungicide once or twice if I see aphids or rust. Last year I got 460 kg per mu of wheat, and if the frost does not hurt it this year I expect about the same.

For summer maize, I plant right after wheat harvest in early June. There is almost no time — sometimes only three or four days — so I plant no-till with the maize seeder behind the tractor. Everyone uses hybrid seed now, you would be crazy not to. I plant about 2.5 kg per mu. At planting I put down about 30 kg of compound fertilizer per mu, then at the big trumpet stage I side-dress 25 kg of urea per mu. That gives me around 16 kg of nitrogen per mu, and about 4 to 5 kg each of phosphate and potash. I do not put as much fertilizer on maize as on wheat because the summer rain usually helps, and the growing season is shorter.

I irrigate maize twice: once when it is jointing, and again when the tassels and silks come out in July or August. If we get a good July rain I might skip one, but the last two summers were dry so I plan for two times. I spray herbicide right after planting, and once more for corn borer if I see the worms in the whorl. I expect about 530 kg per mu from the maize if the wind does not flatten it.

My biggest worry is cost. Fertilizer and electricity for the pump keep going up, and my grandson is in middle school now which means more expenses. But a bad harvest is a disaster I cannot afford, so I would rather waste a little fertilizer than risk losing yield. I watch Lao Wang down the road — if he puts on more urea, I think hard about doing the same. This year I will spend a bit more on wheat because maize prices were decent last season and I have some cash in hand.
